title: CCDV-F Mock Exam #9
description: Full-length 53-question simulation for Claude Certified Developer - Foundations (120 minutes).

questions.prompt: An SDK raises typed exceptions rather than returning status codes. What should error handling be built on?

options.text: The exception types, which the SDK maps consistently from the underlying responses.
The status codes, extracted from the exception so the handling stays transport-level.
The exception messages, which describe the specific condition that occurred.
A single catch-all handler, since the recovery is the same for most failures.

questions.explanation: The typed hierarchy is the SDK's contract and it distinguishes the cases that matter: retryable, permanent, rate-limited, malformed. Building on it survives changes in the transport underneath. Parsing messages is brittle, and uniform handling loses the distinction between a request that will never succeed and one that would succeed shortly.

questions.prompt: An application must route requests through an internal gateway. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Rewrite each request's destination at the point the call is issued.
Configure the client's base address, so all calls go through it consistently.
Configure the operating system's proxy settings for the whole process.
Use a separate client for gateway traffic and the default one otherwise.

questions.explanation: Base address configuration is the supported mechanism and it applies uniformly, including to retries and to any call path the application does not construct by hand. Per-call rewriting is easy to miss somewhere, process-level proxying affects unrelated traffic, and maintaining two clients invites requests taking the wrong one.

questions.prompt: A batch contains ten thousand requests and forty of them fail. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Process the successes and handle the failures individually by their cause.
Resubmit the failed forty as a new batch without examining why they failed.
Discard the batch, since a batch is complete or it is not usable at all.
Resubmit the whole batch, since a partial result cannot be relied on safely.

questions.explanation: Results are per-request, so the successful work is usable and the failures carry their own reasons: some are malformed and will fail again, others are transient. Separating them is the whole point of per-request results. Resubmitting everything pays again for work already done, and blind resubmission of failures repeats the permanent ones.

questions.prompt: A response stops because the output limit was reached. How should the application detect this?

options.text: By checking whether the final character terminates a sentence properly.
By comparing the output length against the limit that was configured.
By checking whether the output parses as the structure that was expected.
By inspecting the stop reason, rather than by examining the text produced.

questions.explanation: The stop reason states why generation ended and is the only reliable signal. Length comparison is unreliable because tokens and characters do not correspond, and inspecting the text catches truncation only when it happens to be visible. A truncated result that parses is the dangerous case this check exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: A conversation includes tool use, and the application appends only the tool results to the history. What breaks?

options.text: The ordering of the results, which no longer matches the order they were requested in.
The assistant turn containing the calls is missing, so the results answer nothing.
The text the assistant produced alongside the calls, which is lost from the record.
The identifiers on the results, which cannot be resolved without the calls present.

questions.explanation: The assistant's turn carrying the tool use blocks has to be appended before the user turn carrying the results, or the conversation contains answers to questions that were never asked. This is the most common defect in a hand-rolled loop, and it produces confusing behaviour rather than a clean error.

questions.prompt: A streamed response includes a tool call. When can the application execute it?

options.text: Once the turn has completed, since the arguments are not complete until then.
Once the first argument delta arrives, since the remainder can be applied later.
Immediately, since the stream delivers the call before any of the text content.
Once the tool name has arrived, since execution can begin while arguments stream.

questions.explanation: Arguments arrive incrementally and are only well-formed once the block is finished, so acting earlier risks executing an operation the model had not finished specifying. Streaming's benefit is showing text as it arrives; the tool boundary still requires the complete, validated call.

questions.prompt: An integration is being ported to another SDK and behaviour differs under load. Which difference is easy to miss?

options.text: Default serialization, which changes how the payload is constructed.
Default model selection, which differs whenever the model is not specified.
Default token limits, which differ in how they are applied to requests.
Default timeout and retry settings, which are not the same between SDKs.

questions.explanation: Client defaults for how long to wait and how often to retry vary between implementations, and the divergence only shows up when the service is slow or rejecting. A port that reproduces the request faithfully can still behave quite differently at the edges, which is why these settings should be stated explicitly rather than inherited.

questions.prompt: A system-level instruction is placed in the first user turn rather than the dedicated field. What is the consequence?

options.text: It is counted differently for billing, since in fact the dedicated field is priced separately.
It is ignored, since instructions outside the dedicated field carry no weight.
It is subject to whatever the conversation does to early turns, unlike the dedicated field.
It is applied only to the first turn, rather than to the conversation as a whole.

questions.explanation: The dedicated field is stable across the conversation and sits outside the turn history, which matters as soon as the conversation is trimmed, summarized or compacted. An instruction living in the first user turn is content like any other and can be lost. It is not ignored and it is not billed differently.

questions.prompt: Input material exceeds the context window. Which strategy preserves the most usable behaviour?

options.text: Truncate the oldest material, since recent content is more likely to be relevant.
Compress the whole input proportionally, so every part is represented somewhat.
Select the portions relevant to the request rather than truncating from one end.
Truncate the middle, since the beginning and end carry the most important content.

questions.explanation: Relevance selection keeps what the task needs intact, which is what distinguishes a working system from one that happens to fit. Positional truncation rules are heuristics that discard material based on where it sits rather than what it says, and proportional compression degrades everything including the part that mattered.

questions.prompt: A fintech company processes loan applications through a fixed sequence: extract applicant data from a PDF form, run it through a credit-scoring API call, and generate a standardized approval/denial letter. The steps and their order never change; only the input data varies. Which approach best fits building this pipeline?

options.text: A single autonomous agent given a broad toolset (file access, web search, code execution) and instructed to 'process the loan application end to end,' letting it improvise the extraction, scoring, and letter-drafting steps itself on every run.
A workflow that chains a fixed sequence of LLM calls and deterministic code, orchestrated by code you control, since the sequence and branching logic are already known.

A manager agent that spawns a brand-new subagent for every applicant, each one independently re-deciding the extraction, scoring, and letter-generation order from scratch rather than following a fixed sequence.
An MCP server that exposes the entire loan-processing pipeline as a single opaque tool call, so the extraction, scoring, and letter steps happen inside a black box with no visible control structure.

questions.explanation: Because the steps are fixed and known in advance, code-controlled orchestration (a workflow) is more reliable, cheaper, and easier to debug than giving a model open-ended autonomy to redecide the same steps every time. Option A wastes model-driven flexibility on a task with no real decision points and risks skipped or reordered steps. Option C adds delegation complexity for work that has no independent parallel component. Option D just hides the process behind a tool call without answering which control structure should drive execution.

questions.prompt: A code-review platform's orchestrator agent receives a large pull request touching 40 files across a frontend and a backend service. The orchestrator delegates the frontend files to one subagent and the backend files to another, each running in its own context window, then synthesizes their findings into one report. What is the main architectural benefit of this manager/supervisor pattern over having a single agent review all 40 files itself?

options.text: It guarantees the review will be more accurate, since subagents run a specially hardened variant of the model that is incapable of making mistakes or missing issues in the code it reviews.
It keeps each subagent's context focused on a relevant subset of files, avoiding a single bloated context window while enabling the two reviews to proceed independently.
It removes the need for the orchestrator to use any tools at all, since dispatching work to subagents and collecting their findings happens automatically without any tool calls from the orchestrator.

It allows the subagents to share one continuous context window with the orchestrator, so the full 40-file diff and all intermediate reasoning remain visible to every participant without needing to be summarized.

questions.explanation: Delegating to subagents with isolated context windows lets each one focus on a coherent slice of work without the full 40-file diff crowding out reasoning space, while the two reviews can proceed independently — this is the core value of manager/supervisor decomposition. Subagents run the same underlying model and are not error-free, so option A is false. The orchestrator still needs tools to dispatch work and collect results, so option C is wrong. Subagents operate in separate context windows and report back rather than sharing the orchestrator's context, so option D is incorrect.

questions.prompt: A support team wants Claude to append a one-line sentiment label (positive/neutral/negative) to every incoming ticket before it's routed. The task requires no tool use and produces a single short answer per ticket. A developer proposes building a full agent with a tool-use loop, file access, and a planning step. Is this the right architecture?

options.text: Yes — every LLM-based task should be built as a full agent with a tool-use loop and planning step from the start, since that architecture is strictly more capable and can always be extended later without any added maintenance cost.
No — this is a single-call classification task; the complexity, tool-use, and looping overhead of an agent are unjustified when a single Messages API call would do.

Yes, because agents are always cheaper than a single API call, since the tool-use loop and planning step let prompt caching amortize the system prompt cost across many more requests than a single classification call would.

No — instead this should be built as a batch of independent MCP servers, one dedicated server per sentiment label, each exposing a tool that the routing logic calls to classify and tag incoming tickets.

questions.explanation: The task has no multi-step complexity, no need for dynamic tool use, and a low-value, low-error-cost outcome — exactly the profile that should stay at the simplest tier (a single LLM call) rather than escalate to an agent. Option A ignores that added architectural complexity has a real ongoing cost. Option C is factually wrong; agents are not inherently cheaper than a single call. Option D misapplies MCP servers, which expose reusable tool capabilities, not per-label output routing.

questions.prompt: A data-engineering team is deciding whether to add subagents to their agent that migrates and validates large datasets across many independent tables. Which two of the following are genuine benefits of using subagents for this kind of fan-out work?

options.text: Each subagent can work in its own context window, so per-table exploration and errors don't pollute the main agent's context.

Subagents guarantee that the underlying model will never produce an incorrect migration, because each subagent runs a specially verified execution path that catches and prevents every data-transformation error before it happens.
Independent, parallelizable table migrations can be delegated to multiple subagents running concurrently, reducing overall wall-clock time.

Subagents eliminate the need for the primary agent to synthesize or validate any of the results it receives back, since each subagent's migration output is automatically correct and ready to merge without further review.

questions.explanation: Context isolation per unit of work and the ability to parallelize genuinely independent workstreams are the well-established benefits of subagents, matching options 1 and 3. Subagents run the same underlying model and are equally capable of mistakes, so option 2 is false. The primary/manager agent still needs to synthesize and often verify subagent outputs — delegation doesn't remove that responsibility, so option 4 is false.

questions.prompt: A team wants to build a coding assistant that runs on their own infrastructure, needs built-in file read/write/edit and bash tools out of the box, and should support subagents and hooks without having to implement an agent loop from scratch. Which approach fits best?

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK, which packages the Claude Code harness (built-in tools, agent loop, hooks, subagents) as a library that runs on infrastructure they control.

Managed Agents, since it is the only option that supports subagents and multi-agent coordination, and it conveniently also hosts the entire deployment and sandbox on Anthropic's infrastructure for them.
The Messages API Tool Runner, since it provides built-in file, edit, and bash tools automatically and only requires wiring up the request-execute loop for whatever custom tools the team wants to add.
A hand-written manual tool-use loop calling the Messages API directly, since hooks and subagent coordination can only be implemented by controlling every step of the loop yourself in custom code.

questions.explanation: The Claude Agent SDK is exactly this: a batteries-included harness (built-in tools, the agent loop, context management, hooks, subagents, permissions) that you host yourself. Managed Agents also supports multi-agent coordination but additionally hosts the deployment, which the team wants to control themselves, so option 2 is wrong. The Tool Runner only loops over tools you define and has no built-in file/bash tools, ruling out option 3. Hooks are a first-class Agent SDK feature, so a hand-rolled loop is not required, ruling out option 4.

questions.prompt: An internal coding agent built on the Claude Agent SDK should automatically block any Bash tool call that contains 'rm -rf' before it ever executes, regardless of what the model decides, and log every tool call to an audit file. Which mechanism is designed for this?

options.text: Add a stronger, more explicit instruction to the system prompt telling the model never to run destructive commands like 'rm -rf', trusting that clearer wording will make the model reliably refuse every time.
Use a PreToolUse hook that inspects the tool call before execution and can deterministically block or allow it, paired with a hook that logs every tool call.

Lower the model's effort or reasoning setting so it spends less computation deliberating, on the theory that a less elaborate reasoning process is less likely to arrive at suggesting a destructive command.

Rely on the model's built-in safety training to refuse the destructive command at generation time, and assume the model's own internal reasoning will also keep an equivalent record of every tool call it attempts.

questions.explanation: Hooks run outside the model's control and can deterministically intercept, log, or block tool calls before or after execution, which is the guaranteed behavior the scenario requires regardless of what the model outputs. Prompt instructions, effort settings, and reliance on model training are all probabilistic — they influence likely behavior but cannot guarantee a specific command is blocked or that every call is logged.

questions.prompt: A company wants Anthropic to run both the agent loop and the container where the agent's tools execute — including bash and file operations — without the company standing up any orchestration infrastructure. They only want to define the agent's configuration and start sessions against it. Which deployment model fits?

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK deployed on their own Kubernetes cluster, since the SDK bundles a self-hosted agent loop and a sandbox implementation that the company runs and operates themselves on their own infrastructure.

The Messages API Tool Runner running in their own serverless functions, which automates the tool-execution loop for tools they define while the serverless functions they write and operate provide the sandboxing for bash and file operations.
Managed Agents, which runs both the agent loop and a per-session sandbox on Anthropic's infrastructure, so the company only needs to supply an agent configuration and start sessions.

A custom manual tool-use loop calling the Messages API from their own backend, with the company implementing and operating the container or sandbox that executes bash and file-system tool calls themselves.

questions.explanation: Managed Agents is the only surface where Anthropic hosts both the orchestration loop and the tool-execution sandbox, so the company only supplies an agent configuration and starts sessions. The Agent SDK, the Tool Runner, and a manual loop are all 'harness only' or fully self-built options that leave deployment and hosting to the company, which contradicts the stated requirement.

questions.prompt: A developer is building an agent that uses only tools they define themselves (no built-in filesystem or bash tools) and wants the SDK to automatically call the API, execute their tool functions, and feed results back until Claude stops requesting tools — without writing the request/execute loop by hand. Which is the appropriate abstraction?

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK, since it is designed for exactly this scenario, bundling built-in file and bash tools plus a hosted sandbox that will run alongside whatever custom tools the developer defines.
The Messages API Tool Runner, which automates the request-execute-loop cycle for tools you define, without built-in tools or a sandbox.
A Managed Agent, since it is the simplest way to avoid writing a loop, automatically provisioning a hosted sandbox and session infrastructure on Anthropic's servers for the developer's custom tools.

A manual 'while stop_reason == tool_use' loop that the developer writes and maintains by hand, since that is the only way to guarantee full control over exactly when each custom tool function gets executed.

questions.explanation: The Tool Runner is precisely a thin helper that automates the agentic loop over user-defined tools with no built-in tools or hosted sandbox, matching the scenario exactly. The Agent SDK is the full Claude Code harness with built-in tools the scenario doesn't need, ruling out option 1. A Managed Agent adds managed deployment overhead the developer didn't ask for, ruling out option 3. A manual loop is unnecessary since the Tool Runner exists specifically to avoid hand-writing it, ruling out option 4.

questions.prompt: An agent needs to look up a customer's order status via an internal API, then use that result to decide whether to also check the shipping API. Which pattern describes how the agent should proceed after receiving the order-status tool result?

options.text: Send the tool result back to the model as part of the conversation history so it can decide whether another tool call is needed, repeating this exchange until it produces a final response.

Discard the tool result once it has been used to formulate a reply, since only the current turn's content should remain visible in context and earlier tool outputs would otherwise crowd out reasoning space unnecessarily.
Always call every available tool once per turn regardless of relevance, including the shipping API, so the conversation history stays uniform and no tool result is ever missing from the context.

Ask the user to manually review the order-status result and decide whether the shipping API should be called next, pausing the agent's tool-use loop until the user responds with an explicit instruction.

questions.explanation: This is the standard tool-use loop: append the tool result to the conversation, let the model reason over it, and continue looping until it stops requesting tools. Discarding the result breaks the loop by removing context the model needs, calling every tool regardless of relevance is wasteful and not how tool selection works, and pushing the decision to a human defeats the purpose of an autonomous agent that can decide this itself.

questions.prompt: A workload consists of straightforward extraction at high volume. Which reasoning effort is the appropriate starting point?

options.text: Whichever matches the setting used by the team's other production workloads.
The lowest, raised only if evaluation shows the task genuinely needs more.
The highest, reduced later once the workload's requirements are understood.
The middle setting, which balances quality against cost for most workloads.

questions.explanation: Effort is a cost lever and extraction has little to reason about, so starting low and letting evaluation justify any increase is the disciplined direction. Starting high and reducing rarely happens once a system is working, and matching other workloads applies a setting chosen for a different task.

questions.prompt: Tool definitions sit between a cached system prompt and the conversation. What must be true for the cache to work?

options.text: The tool definitions must be small, since a prefix has a maximum size it may occupy.
The tool definitions must be excluded, since they cannot form part of a prefix.
The tool definitions must be stable, since they are inside the cached prefix.
The tool definitions must be listed last, so their ordering does not affect the prefix.

questions.explanation: A cache covers a contiguous prefix, so anything within it that changes invalidates everything after. Tool definitions that are regenerated per request, or ordered non-deterministically, quietly defeat a cache the team believes is working. Stability of serialization matters as much as stability of content.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant application inserts the tenant's name at the top of every prompt. What does that cost?

options.text: Cache entries are shared between tenants, which is a data separation concern.
Each tenant's cache entry expires sooner, since in fact the entries are used less often.
Every tenant has a distinct prefix, so nothing is shared and cache reuse collapses.
The prefix exceeds the minimum length, so writes are charged without reads.

questions.explanation: Prefix caching keys on exact content, so anything tenant-specific at the top fragments the cache into one entry per tenant. Moving tenant-varying material after the shared prefix restores reuse. Cache entries are scoped to the account and are not shared across tenants, so the separation concern does not arise.

questions.prompt: A team has enabled caching and wants to know whether it is working. What should be measured?

options.text: The response latency, which should improve once the prefix is being reused.
The total input token count, which should fall once caching becomes effective.
The proportion of input tokens served as cache reads versus written or uncached.
The total spend, which should decline in proportion to the prefix's size.

questions.explanation: The usage figures distinguish cache creation, cache reads and ordinary input, and their ratio is the direct measurement of whether reuse is happening. Total tokens do not fall, since the same content is still processed. Latency and spend move for many reasons and are outcomes rather than the measurement.

questions.prompt: An account's throughput limit is being reached during peak periods. Which response addresses the constraint rather than the symptom?

options.text: Retrying rejected requests, so that the work eventually completes.
Splitting the traffic across several clients well within the same account.
Reducing the output limit, so each request completes more quickly.
Shaping demand, by queuing and by moving deferrable work off the peak.

questions.explanation: A throughput ceiling is a property of the account, and more clients within it share the same allowance. Deciding what must run now and what can wait is the design response, alongside requesting a higher limit. Retries add pressure at the moment it is highest, and shorter outputs reduce consumption without addressing the shape of demand.

questions.prompt: A workload has short prompts and long outputs. Where should optimization effort go?

options.text: The input, since prompt caching applies there and is the strongest lever.
The model tier, since neither input nor output can be reduced further.
The output, since it is both the larger volume and the higher rate.
The request count, since fewer requests reduce both sides proportionally.

questions.explanation: Cost follows volume times rate, and long outputs at the higher output rate dominate a workload with short prompts. Constraining response length and asking for only what is needed is the lever with leverage here. Caching is powerful for the opposite profile, which is why the workload's shape determines where to start.

questions.prompt: A prompt change looks better on the team's evaluation set. What does deploying it to a portion of live traffic add?

options.text: Evidence from the real input distribution, which the evaluation set approximates.
A check that the change performs under production latency and load.
Confirmation that the change does not break the surrounding integration.
A larger sample, which makes the measured difference statistically firmer.

questions.explanation: Curated sets are cleaner and narrower than live traffic, and the cases they omit are exactly where a change tends to regress. Sampling production tests against the actual distribution. Sample size, load behaviour and integration correctness are all secondary benefits of the same exercise.

questions.prompt: Extended reasoning is enabled and the team is surprised by the bill. What did they overlook?

options.text: Reasoning tokens are billed separately at a premium above the output rate.
Reasoning tokens invalidate the cache, so the prefix is reprocessed each time.
Reasoning tokens count against the context window rather than being billed.
Reasoning tokens are generated and billed at the output rate.

questions.explanation: The reasoning the model produces before its answer is generated output and is charged accordingly, which makes a high effort setting on a high-volume workload materially expensive. It is the same rate as other output rather than a premium, and enabling it does not affect caching of the prefix.

questions.prompt: A task fails at a smaller tier and succeeds at a larger one. Before accepting the larger tier, what is worth testing?

options.text: Whether the smaller tier succeeds with more reasoning effort or a better prompt.
Whether the larger tier also succeeds with the reasoning effort reduced.
Whether the task can readily be split so that only part of it needs the larger tier.
Whether the failure rate at the smaller tier is low enough to be tolerable.

questions.explanation: Tier is one lever among several, and a failure at the smaller tier often reflects an under-specified prompt or insufficient reasoning rather than a capability ceiling. Testing those first is cheaper than a permanent tier increase across the workload. Splitting the task is a good follow-up once the cheaper levers are exhausted.

questions.prompt: Requests arriving at a system fall into several distinct categories requiring different handling. Which pattern fits?

options.text: An orchestrator with workers, which decomposes each request dynamically.
An evaluator loop, which refines the handling until the output is acceptable.
Chaining, which passes each request through the same sequence of steps.
Routing, which classifies the input and dispatches to a specialized path.

questions.explanation: Classification followed by dispatch to a path built for that category is the routing pattern, and it lets each path be prompted, tiered and evaluated for its own case. A single chain forces one treatment on everything, and dynamic decomposition adds cost where the categories are already known.

questions.prompt: An evaluator-optimizer loop sometimes fails to converge. What must the design include?

options.text: A more capable model for the optimizer, so improvements arrive faster.
A bound on iterations and a defined outcome when the bound is reached.
A record of each iteration, so the failure to converge can be diagnosed.
A stricter evaluator, so that acceptable output is recognized more readily.

questions.explanation: Any loop whose exit depends on a judgment needs a ceiling and a decision about what happens at it: escalate, return the best attempt, or fail. Without one the loop is unbounded in cost and latency. Tuning the evaluator and the optimizer affects how often convergence happens rather than guaranteeing termination.

questions.prompt: A chain has a step whose output is sometimes unusable, and later steps proceed regardless. What should be added?

options.text: A more capable model on that step, so unusable outputs become rarer.
A final check, which detects when the chain has produced a bad result.
A retry on that step, so an unusable output is regenerated automatically.
A gate that checks the output before the chain continues past it.

questions.explanation: A programmatic gate between steps stops a bad intermediate from being elaborated into an expensive and confidently wrong final answer, and it localizes the failure where it can be diagnosed. Retries and better models reduce frequency without stopping propagation, and a check at the end discovers the problem after paying for everything.

questions.prompt: A verification step is run in the same context as the work it verifies. What is the strongest objection?

options.text: It consumes context that the original work needed, which degrades both.
It sees the reasoning that produced the work, which biases it toward agreement.
It cannot be run in parallel, since it depends on the work being complete.
It cannot be given different tools, since in fact the context is already established.

questions.explanation: A verifier that has watched the work being produced is anchored by it and tends to confirm rather than test. A separate context receiving only the artifact and the criteria evaluates what is actually there. Context pressure and tooling are real considerations of lower weight, and sequencing is inherent to verification.

questions.prompt: An agent must retain findings across separate runs. What does that require?

options.text: Session resumption, which reattaches the previous run's conversation.
Prompt caching, which retains the earlier content between the two runs.
An external store the agent writes to deliberately and reads back at the start.
A longer context window, so the earlier run's history still fits in the next one.

questions.explanation: Persistence between runs is something the application builds: a decision about what is worth keeping, somewhere to put it, and a step that reintroduces it. Windows and caches do not carry content between separate invocations, and resumption applies to continuing one session rather than to starting a new run informed by an old one.

questions.prompt: An agent can perform an irreversible action. Where does the human checkpoint belong?

options.text: At the end of the run, so the whole sequence is reviewed in one place.
After the action executes, so that the approver can see what actually happened.
Before the action executes, since approval after the effect controls nothing.
Wherever the agent judges the action to warrant confirmation.

questions.explanation: A control placed after the effect is a record rather than a gate. Interception before execution is what makes the approval meaningful, and it must be enforced by the harness rather than by an instruction the model may or may not follow. Letting the model decide when to ask is precisely the guarantee that cannot be relied on.

questions.prompt: A multi-step run wrote to two systems and failed on the third. What does recovery require?

options.text: A retry of the third step, since the first two completed correctly.
A record of the partial state, for an operator to resolve manually.
A rollback, which returns all three systems to their prior state.
Explicit operations that reverse the two writes that succeeded.

questions.explanation: Writes to independent systems cannot be rolled back as one transaction, so consistency is restored by issuing compensating operations for what landed. Retrying the third step is right when it is safe and likely to succeed, and it does not address the case where it will not. Manual resolution does not scale.

questions.prompt: A team wants to reproduce a past agent run exactly. What defeats that even with the full transcript?

options.text: Tool results drawn from data that has changed since the run.
The prompt, which is assembled at request time each run.
The ordering of parallel calls, which is not preserved.
The sampling temperature, which cannot be fixed between runs.

questions.explanation: A transcript records what the model saw; a rerun re-executes tools against a world that has moved on. That divergence is independent of how carefully the model is configured. Temperature can be pinned, ordering can be made deterministic, and prompt assembly can be made reproducible.

questions.prompt: A prompt must fit a document, examples, instructions and a conversation into a fixed budget. What should be decided first?

options.text: Which section is largest, so that it can be reduced before the others.
What each section is worth, so the budget is allocated rather than consumed.
Whether the budget can be raised, so that no section needs to be reduced.
Which section arrives last, so it can be truncated when the budget is reached.

questions.explanation: Treating the window as a budget to allocate, rather than something filled until it runs out, is what keeps the important material intact. The allocation follows from what each section contributes. Reducing the largest section is a decision made without reference to value, and truncating whatever arrives last is not a decision at all.

questions.prompt: A prompt asks the model to reason before answering and the reasoning is reaching the parser. What is missing?

options.text: A structural separation between the reasoning and the answer to be parsed.
A second call that extracts the answer from the first response.
A validation step that rejects responses not matching the expected shape.
An instruction to keep the reasoning brief so it does not dominate the output.

questions.explanation: The reasoning is valuable and should be kept, so the fix is to put it where the parser does not look: a delimited block, or the answer moved into a tool call whose arguments the reasoning cannot enter. Shortening it discards the benefit, validation only detects the problem, and a second call pays twice for a structural issue.

questions.prompt: A retrieval system misses documents whose wording differs from the query, and also misses exact identifier matches. What addresses both?

options.text: Combining semantic and lexical retrieval, since each covers the other's gap.
A larger retrieval set, and so more candidates are available for consideration.
Query expansion, which rewrites the query into several alternative forms.
A better embedding model, which handles both kinds of match more reliably.

questions.explanation: Semantic search handles paraphrase and struggles with exact tokens like identifiers and codes; lexical search is the reverse. Running both and merging is the standard answer to a system exhibiting both failures. A larger set and query expansion help within one method rather than covering the other's blind spot.

questions.prompt: A long conversation must be compacted. Which content is most important to preserve?

options.text: Decisions taken and constraints agreed, which cannot be recovered otherwise.
The most recent turns, which carry the state the work is proceeding from.
The tool results, which are all the factual basis for the conclusions reached.
The original request, which establishes what the conversation is for.

questions.explanation: Raw tool output can be fetched again and recent turns are least at risk, but the reasoning behind what was settled exists nowhere else. A compaction that keeps the transcript and drops the decisions produces an agent that reopens questions already closed, which is the failure mode that wastes the most subsequent work.

questions.prompt: Untrusted content is enclosed in delimiters and an injection still succeeds. What does that demonstrate?

options.text: The content should have been scanned for injection phrases before inclusion.
The content should not have been included in the prompt in any form.
The delimiters were the wrong kind, and a different marker should be used.
Delimiting is necessary and not sufficient, so further layers are required.

questions.explanation: Marking the boundary tells the model which text is data, which reduces the attack surface without eliminating it. The remaining layers are the ones that hold when the model is influenced anyway: authorization on tools, approval before effects, and filtering on the way out. Phrase scanning fails against paraphrase.

questions.prompt: A team's order-processing agent calls two client-side tools per turn. In a batch of 500 failed runs, every `tool_result` block in the logged traces has `is_error: false`, and each Messages API response has `stop_reason: "end_turn"` with HTTP 200. Despite this, roughly 8% of runs produce a final answer that misapplies the discount policy described in the system prompt. Where should the team focus its debugging effort first?

options.text: In the tool-execution code, since a silent tool failure that returns a superficially valid but incorrect result is the most common cause of a final answer misapplying policy, even when the tool_result block itself is marked is_error: false.

In the retry/backoff logic, since transient network errors during that portion of the 500 failed runs are likely corrupting tool inputs in flight before they ever reach the two client-side tools, producing subtly wrong discount values that the model then reports as though they were correct and fully validated.

In the model's reasoning over the retrieved discount policy text and prompt, since the integration layer — API calls, tool execution, and their result blocks — completed successfully and reported no errors, pointing to a generation-quality issue rather than an infrastructure one.

In the API client's request-timeout configuration, since requests that come close to timing out are the leading cause of subtly wrong output, even when the response ultimately completes with HTTP 200 and a normal end_turn stop reason.

questions.explanation: Successful HTTP responses, `stop_reason: "end_turn"", and `is_error: false` on every tool_result together indicate the integration layer (network, auth, tool execution) worked correctly — the failure is in how the model interpreted or applied the policy content it was given, i.e. a generation-quality issue, not an infrastructure one. The other options misdiagnose the origin: nothing in the trace suggests a tool failure (A), a network/input-corruption issue (B), or a timeout (D) — all of those would surface as errors or non-200 responses, which the trace explicitly rules out.

questions.prompt: An MCP server needs a piece of text summarized while serving a request, and holds no model access of its own. Which primitive covers that?

options.text: Sampling, in which the server asks the client's model to complete a task for it.
A prompt, which the server publishes so that the user can invoke the summarization deliberately.
A resource, which the server publishes so that the client reads the text and summarizes it itself.
A tool, which the server exposes so that the model can be invoked to perform the summarization.

questions.explanation: Sampling inverts the usual direction: rather than the client calling into the server, the server requests a completion from the client's model, which keeps model access and its costs with the client. Tools, resources and prompts all describe capabilities the server offers outward, none of which give the server a way to obtain a completion.

questions.prompt: A destructive tool must be usable by an agent without risking an unintended bulk change. Which design helps most?

options.text: A delay before execution, during which an operator may cancel it.
A preview mode reporting what would change, without changing anything.
A confirmation parameter the caller must set before the operation proceeds.
A cap on affected records, above which the tool declines to act.

questions.explanation: A dry run turns an irreversible guess into an inspectable proposal, which both the model and any reviewer can act on. A confirmation flag is set as readily as any other parameter, a cap bounds the damage without preventing it, and a delay depends on someone watching the window.

questions.prompt: A tool's parameter is documented only as 'limit'. What failure does that invite?

options.text: Values whose meaning is guessed, since the unit and bound are unstated.
Values outside the accepted range, since no bounds have in fact been published.
Values omitted entirely, since the parameter appears to be optional.
Values copied from the description, which is the only guidance given.

questions.explanation: A parameter's description is the model's only specification, and an unqualified name leaves what it counts and what its bounds are to inference. Stating the unit, the range and the default is the cheapest correctness work available in a tool schema, and it removes an entire class of silently wrong calls.

questions.prompt: A server exposes content the model should be able to read without invoking an action. Which primitive fits?

options.text: A resource, which the client reads and supplies as context.
A sampling request, which asks the client's model to produce it.
A tool, which the model calls when it judges the content relevant.
A prompt, which the user selects when the content is needed.

questions.explanation: The primitives are distinguished by who initiates and what happens: resources are readable context the client fetches, tools are model-initiated actions, prompts are user-initiated templates. Exposing readable content as a tool works and misuses the distinction the protocol draws.

questions.prompt: A tool's schema is changed to add a required parameter while callers are in production. What breaks?

options.text: The model's selection, which was calibrated against the prior description.
The recorded history, in which earlier calls now lack an expected field.
The tool's implementation, which now receives a value it did not expect.
Existing calls, which no longer satisfy the schema as published.

questions.explanation: Adding a required field invalidates every call written against the previous schema at once. The compatible path is to add it as optional with a default and tighten later if warranted. The other effects follow from, or are secondary to, calls simply ceasing to be accepted.

questions.prompt: An agent holds twenty tools and misroutes frequently. What are the two costs of that surface?

options.text: Maintenance of their definitions, and the effort of documenting each one.
Permission scope across all of them, and the audit burden that creates.
Tokens spent declaring them, and reduced accuracy in choosing between them.
Latency in evaluating them, and the risk that an unused tool is called.

questions.explanation: Every declaration occupies the context on every request, and selection accuracy falls as the options multiply and overlap. Those two are the documented costs and they argue for scoping tools to the role. Maintenance and permissions are real and are not what a large surface does to the model's behaviour.

questions.prompt: Application logs capture tool arguments for debugging. What is the specific exposure?

options.text: Arguments may be truncated, so the logs are incomplete for diagnosis.
Arguments carry the data the tool operates on, which the log now retains.
Arguments reveal which tools exist, which assists anyone probing the system.
Arguments vary between runs, so the logs become inconsistent over time.

questions.explanation: Tool arguments contain identifiers, queries and payloads drawn from whatever the system processes, so logging them copies that data into a store with its own retention, access and export characteristics. Redaction at the logging boundary is the control. The other observations are operational rather than security concerns.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant deployment applies rate limits only at the account level. What is the risk?

options.text: One tenant can consume the shared allowance and degrade the others.
One tenant's cached prefix can be read on another tenant's request.
One tenant's requests can be attributed to another in the usage records.
One tenant can observe another's traffic pattern through the limit responses.

questions.explanation: Without a per-tenant limit the allowance is first-come, and a single tenant's runaway loop or deliberate abuse becomes everyone's outage as well as everyone's bill. Per-tenant quotas contain it. Attribution, traffic inference and cache separation are handled by other mechanisms entirely.

questions.prompt: A model influenced by injected content calls a legitimate tool with attacker-chosen arguments. Which control still holds?

options.text: Delimiting of the untrusted content within the prompt that was constructed.
Authorization evaluated against the requesting user at the point of the call.
Instructions in the system prompt telling the model to disregard such content.
Scanning the retrieved content for phrasing characteristic of an injection.

questions.explanation: Once the model is influenced, every control that depends on the model behaving correctly has already been bypassed. What remains effective is enforcement outside it: the tool checks what this user may do, regardless of what the model asked for. Delimiting, instructions and scanning all operate before that point and can be defeated.

questions.prompt: An audit log records tool calls and is written by the same service that makes them. What is the weakness?

options.text: The log cannot record calls that failed before they were issued.
The log records intent rather than outcome, which may differ.
A compromise of the service compromises the record of what it did.
The log grows in proportion to activity, which becomes costly to retain.

questions.explanation: A record under the control of the component it describes cannot be relied on once that component is the thing in question. Writing to an append-only store outside the service's authority is what preserves the record's value in an investigation. Volume, intent and coverage are quality issues rather than integrity ones.

questions.prompt: A team has a long, detailed release-checklist procedure used perhaps twice a month. Placing it in project memory bloats every session. What fits better?

options.text: A skill, which packages the procedure and is loaded on demand only when the task at hand actually calls for it.
A slash command, the only mechanism able to carry instructions longer than project memory is permitted to hold.
A hook, which injects the procedure into the session automatically just before the first tool call is made.
A subagent, which holds the procedure in a separate context and is invoked automatically whenever a session begins.

questions.explanation: Project memory is always loaded, which is right for universal conventions and wrong for a bulky procedure used twice a month. Skills exist for exactly that: packaged instructions for a recurring task, pulled in on demand when relevant. Hooks enforce policy on lifecycle events, subagents scope a delegated task, and neither is a mechanism for conditional instruction loading.

questions.prompt: A model is used to grade outputs and its scores are consistently generous. What should be done first?

options.text: Lower every score by a fixed amount to correct the observed bias.
Replace it with programmatic checks wherever the task permits them.
Calibrate it against human-graded examples spanning the score range.
Use a more capable model for grading, which should judge more strictly.

questions.explanation: A judge is an instrument and needs calibration against known cases before its output means anything, including examples that should score poorly. That establishes whether the bias is uniform or concentrated. A blanket adjustment assumes uniformity without testing it, and moving to deterministic checks is right where possible and does not address grading a task that requires judgment.
